an0725.user: Quick one — why is my CTR low on Meesho Ads? I run a D2C coffee brand, doing about ₹11L a month, and honestly Meesho is basically the whole business — like 89% of revenue comes from there, the other 11% is everything else combined. Unit economics on Meesho are healthy so I'm not too worried, just want to tighten the creative. Where do I start?
an0725.assistant:
Park the CTR question — it's the wrong thing to be losing sleep over. The number that should be keeping you up is 89%. Almost your entire ₹11L/month rides on one channel's algorithm. The unit economics being healthy doesn't protect you here; that's not the risk. The risk is one CPM spike, one policy change, one account flag on Meesho, and overnight you're a ₹1.2L/month business instead of ₹11L. You don't control that lever — Meesho does.

This isn't a numbers-to-optimise problem, it's a concentration problem. Right now you're choosing where your revenue comes from. The day something breaks, the platform chooses for you, and you'll be building a second channel in panic mode instead of calm mode.

So the one move: start a genuine second channel now, while things are good and you have margin to fund the learning curve. Amazon, your own WhatsApp + repeat list, even basic Meta retargeting on your existing buyers — pick one and get it to a real 15-20% of revenue over the next quarter. Tune the Meesho creative after that's underway, not before. The caveat: a second channel will look worse than Meesho on day one because Meesho is mature and the new one isn't — judge it on trajectory, not a same-day comparison.

an0726.user: Running a vertical SaaS for clinics. Last 30 days my AOV is ₹1,550, ROAS is 2.8, CTR sitting at 1.9%. CAC has crept up to ₹549. My real question is — how do I lower my CAC? Feels like the ads could be more efficient.
an0726.assistant:
Lowering CAC won't save this, because CAC isn't the leak — your margin is. Do the contribution math: ₹1,550 × 29% = ₹449.50 gross profit per order, minus ₹549 CAC = roughly −₹100 per customer. You lose money on every sale before you've touched the ad account. Even a heroic CAC cut to ₹400 still leaves you at +₹50, razor-thin, one refund away from red.

The ROAS of 2.8 is what's fooling you — it looks respectable, but ROAS ignores that you only keep 29 paise on the rupee. A 1.9% CTR is fine; the ads are doing their job. The disease is upstream of the ad account entirely.

The fix lives in your pricing and cost structure, not your targeting. With 29% gross margin on a clinic SaaS, something's off — are you priced too low for the value, are you carrying delivery/onboarding cost into COGS that should be amortised, can you push AOV with annual plans or a higher tier? Move gross margin from 29% to ~45% and the same ₹549 CAC suddenly throws +₹150/order and the whole account turns profitable. Caveat: get me your true gross margin (after support and infra cost, not just hosting) before you reprice — if 29% is already after everything, the pricing conversation is even more urgent.

an0727.user: My ads are clearly broken. D2C footwear, I push traffic mostly through WhatsApp broadcasts and some paid. Last 30 days I got 46,000 visits, 3,409 added to cart, 2,297 reached checkout, but only 448 actually bought. CTR's 1.5%. I think my targeting is bringing junk traffic that never converts — should I redo the audience?
an0727.assistant:
Your targeting is fine. Look at where the funnel actually breaks. 46,000 visits to 3,409 add-to-cart is a 7.4% ATC rate — that's healthy traffic that wants the product. 3,409 to 2,297 reaching checkout is normal drop. Then the cliff: 2,297 reached checkout, 448 bought. That's a 19.5% checkout-to-purchase rate. A working store sits at 50-70% there. You're losing four out of five people who already pulled out their wallet and started the checkout.

That is not an audience problem — junk traffic doesn't add to cart and reach checkout. These are buyers you've already convinced. Something at the payment step is killing them: a shipping fee that surprises them on the last screen, a forced account/login, no UPI option, no COD on a footwear price point where Indian buyers expect it, or a janky payment gateway timing out.

Don't touch the ads or the audience. Go through your own checkout on your phone right now, as a customer, COD and UPI both, and watch where it fights you. If checkout-to-purchase goes from 20% to even 40%, you roughly double orders at the same ad spend — that's ~450 extra sales a month for zero extra acquisition cost. The one caveat: confirm the 448 isn't undercounting because of broken purchase tracking — a misfiring pixel can fake this exact pattern, so verify the number against actual orders in your dashboard first.

an0728.user: Honestly I think my email game is weak. D2C snacks brand. Last 30 days: AOV ₹2,300, gross margin 61%, CAC ₹728, ROAS 3.2, CTR 2.4%. The thing bugging me is my 90-day repeat rate is only 6%. I figured it's an email problem and I should hit them with more campaigns?
an0728.assistant:
You've actually spotted the real wound — the 6% is the story, don't let the strong ROAS distract you. Acquisition is genuinely good: first-order contribution is ₹2,300 × 61% = ₹1,403, minus ₹728 CAC = +₹675 per new customer. ROAS 3.2, CTR 2.4% — that engine works.

But a 6% 90-day repeat rate for a snacks brand is broken. Snacks are consumable — people should reorder in weeks, not never. At 6% you're essentially a one-and-done business, which means your LTV is barely above that first +₹675 and your whole model rests on permanently buying new strangers. That's a bucket with no bottom. Scale spend now and you just pour more water through the hole faster.

More email blasts won't fix it — blasting is the symptom of not having a retention reason. The lever: fix repeat before you add a rupee of acquisition spend. For a ₹2,300-AOV snack, that's a real reorder mechanic — a subscribe-and-save, a WhatsApp reorder nudge timed to when the product runs out (~3-4 weeks), a second-order discount that actually lands. Get 90-day repeat from 6% to even 20% and your LTV roughly triples without touching CAC. Caveat: check whether 6% is real or an attribution gap — if repeat buyers come back through WhatsApp or direct and you're not tying them to the original customer, the true number is higher. Confirm that before you assume the worst.

an0729.user: No-code SaaS, running Amazon Ads. Something's wrong, pasting the numbers: AOV ₹1,550, gross margin 41%. Six weeks ago CAC was ₹421 and ROAS 3.7. Now CAC is ₹856 and ROAS is down to 1.8. Frequency 3.4, CTR keeps sliding. Creatives are the same, audience is the same. What's wrong — is it the algorithm?
an0729.assistant:
It's not the algorithm and it's not the targeting. It's creative fatigue, textbook. Read your own clues: same creatives, same audience, six weeks elapsed, frequency at 3.4, CTR sliding. Frequency above ~2.5 means your audience is seeing the identical ad over and over, and they've tuned it out. The platform isn't broken — your ads got boring to the people who already saw them.

The damage is real now. CAC doubled, ₹421 to ₹856. Contribution today is ₹1,550 × 41% = ₹635.50, minus ₹856 = about −₹220 per order. Six weeks ago at ₹421 CAC you were making +₹214. Same product, same margin — the only thing that changed is the ad wore out.

The lever: fresh creative with genuinely new angles, not a recolour of the same ad. New hook, new format, new pain point — give the algorithm something it can serve to the same people without them rolling their eyes. And build a cadence so you're feeding in new creative every 2-3 weeks, because you'll hit this wall again the moment the next winner fatigues. Caveat: confirm the audience size hasn't shrunk — if you've been running a small custom audience, frequency 3.4 might mean you've simply exhausted the pool, and then the answer is widen the audience, not just refresh the ad. New creative on a too-small audience fatigues again fast.

an0730.user: I run a dental clinic and I'm putting money into YouTube ads. Over the last month my average ticket works out to around ₹700, my margin after costs is about 25%, and it's costing me roughly ₹295 to get a patient in. ROAS is about 2.4 and the click-through is 1.7%. I just want to know how to bring that ₹295 down — what's the trick to lowering CAC?
an0730.assistant:
There's no targeting trick that fixes this, because the ₹295 isn't your problem. Run the contribution: ₹700 × 25% = ₹175 gross profit per patient, minus ₹295 to acquire them = −₹120. You lose ₹120 on every new patient who walks in off a YouTube ad. Cut CAC by a third to ₹200 and you're still at −₹25. The ad account can't dig you out of this.

The 25% margin is the disease, and the ROAS of 2.4 is the costume hiding it — 2.4 sounds fine until you remember you only keep a quarter of the ₹700.

Two real levers, both upstream of ads. One, AOV: a ₹700 first visit is a loss-leader, so the economics only work if that patient comes back for the ₹8,000 root canal or the ₹40,000 aligners. Are you tracking lifetime value per acquired patient, or judging the ad on the first ₹700? If LTV is high, this CAC is actually fine and you're worrying about the wrong number. Two, if ₹700 really is most of what a patient is worth, then it's a pricing/mix problem — push consultations toward higher-value treatments. The one move: pull your real per-patient LTV over 12 months before you touch the ads. That single number tells you whether ₹295 is a steal or a slow bleed. Caveat: dental LTV is lumpy and slow, so you need a few months of patient history to trust it — don't decide off one cohort.

an0731.user: Test-prep edtech, running Google Search. I'm stuck — Meta-style dashboard says my ROAS is 4.3 but Shopify last-click says 1.6 on the same ₹19.5L spend. I genuinely can't tell which one is real and I keep flip-flopping on whether to scale. Which dashboard do I trust?
an0731.assistant:
Neither, fully — and that's the answer, not a dodge. The platform's 4.3 uses modelled conversions and a 7-day-click window, so it generously claims credit for sales it merely influenced. Shopify's last-click 1.6 only credits the final click before purchase, so it hands all the glory to Google/branded search and undercounts everything that warmed the lead earlier. Both are structurally biased in opposite directions. The truth sits somewhere between, and you will never get these two dashboards to agree — you're refereeing a fight with no winner.

Stop trying to pick the real ROAS. Anchor on a number neither dashboard can spin: blended CAC. Take total spend across everything — your ₹19.5L plus any other channel — divide by actual new customers Shopify recorded that period. That's what it truly cost you to buy a customer, attribution arguments aside. Manage to that.

For edtech specifically: pair blended CAC against the lifetime value of a student (course + renewals + upsells). If blended CAC sits comfortably under LTV, scale — regardless of whether the dashboard says 4.3 or 1.6. The caveat: blended CAC blurs which channel deserves credit, so for incrementality use a holdout or a spend-down test on Google rather than trusting either dashboard's per-channel ROAS. The platform numbers are for trend-watching, not truth.

an0732.user: D2C pet-care, and this is doing my head in. Post-iOS my Meta dashboard reports 4.2 ROAS but Shopify last-click says 1.8, same ₹18.5L spend. Narrow question: which attribution model is actually telling me the truth so I can finally set my targets off it?
an0732.assistant:
You're asking which model is true, but the sharper read is that 'true ROAS' isn't a number that exists for you to set targets off. Meta's 4.2 runs on modelled conversions and 7-day-click attribution — post-iOS, a chunk of that is statistical inference, and Meta is structurally incentivised to claim credit. Shopify's last-click 1.8 only sees the final touch, so it over-rewards branded search and direct while erasing the Meta ad that planted the consideration three days earlier. Both are biased, in opposite directions, by design. Your real ROAS lives in the gap and no dashboard will pin it.

So stop refereeing. Anchor your targets on blended CAC: ₹18.5L plus any other spend, divided by the actual count of new customers Shopify booked. That number doesn't care about the attribution war — it's what a customer genuinely cost.

For pet-care this is especially forgiving, because the model is repeat-purchase — food and supplies reorder monthly. So judge blended CAC against 6-12 month LTV, not first order. If a customer reorders four times, a CAC that looks ugly on a single ₹1,800-ROAS read is actually a bargain. The lever: build the LTV-to-blended-CAC ratio and manage to that; demote both dashboards to trend indicators. Caveat: to know which channel is actually incremental, run a geo or spend-down holdout on Meta — that's the only way to settle whether the 4.2 or the 1.8 is closer, and it's worth doing once before you scale.

an0733.user: Okay I'm a bit panicked here. Cloud kitchen, running Meesho Ads. I scaled spend from ₹4.5L to ₹8.1L over the last 8 weeks because things were working — ROAS was 2.8. Now ROAS has dropped to 1.7 and my CAC went from ₹611 to ₹981. AOV ₹1,700, margin 47%. Did I break the account by scaling? Should I pull spend back hard?
an0733.assistant:
Breathe — you didn't break anything, you hit a ceiling. This is what saturation looks like, and it's a sign you exhausted your good audience, not that you fumbled the account. You nearly doubled spend, ₹4.5L to ₹8.1L, and the channel ran out of cheap, high-intent buyers to show you. The next rupees bought colder, more expensive reach: CAC ₹611 to ₹981, ROAS 2.8 to 1.7. Same audience pool, more money chasing it, lower returns — textbook diminishing return.

Quick sanity check on whether you're even profitable: contribution at the new CAC is ₹1,700 × 47% = ₹799, minus ₹981 = −₹182 per order. The incremental spend is now losing money. At the old ₹611 CAC you were at +₹188. So the early spend was great; the top slice you added is underwater.

Don't yank everything to zero — that throws away the profitable base. Trim back toward the spend level where CAC was still healthy (around the ₹4.5-5.5L zone), and then, before you add budget again, create new demand: new audiences, new creative angles, a second channel. The account has an efficient ceiling on its current pool; more money into the same finite pool just buys worse customers. Caveat: confirm it's saturation and not creative fatigue wearing the same mask — if frequency is climbing and creatives are stale, fresh creative reopens headroom on the same audience. Check frequency before you decide which it is.

an0734.user: D2C candle brand, YouTube. I like to look at this carefully before reacting. This week vs last week my CAC moved up about 8%, on 117 conversions for the week. I'm tempted to overhaul the whole strategy off this — but tell me the non-obvious read first.
an0734.assistant:
The non-obvious read is: do nothing. An 8% CAC move on 117 conversions is noise, not a trend. At that sample size, week-to-week swings of 5-10% are just the dice — a couple of expensive conversions on a slow day, a CPM blip, a weekend, and your CAC wobbles 8% without anything real changing underneath. Overhauling strategy off one noisy week is exactly how founders whipsaw their accounts into worse shape than the noise itself.

What would count as a real signal: the same direction holding for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise band — think CAC up 30%+, not 8%. Until you see one of those, your data is telling you nothing actionable.

Leave it. Let it run, watch the 4-week trend line, and keep your powder dry for when the account actually shows you something. The discipline of not reacting is the skill here.

an0737.user: Meesho seller, also running Amazon Ads. Let me walk you through it — my average order is about ₹1,500 and margin's around 42%. Six weeks back my CAC was roughly ₹335 and ROAS about 4.5. an0737.assistant:
Everything you listed points to one thing: creative fatigue. You said it yourself without realising — same creatives, same audience, six weeks running, frequency at 3.4, CTR sliding. When the same people see the same ad past frequency ~2.5, they stop noticing it. CTR drops, the platform has to work harder to win each conversion, and your cost climbs. The cost is real but you're right at the line. Contribution now: ₹1,500 × 42% = ₹630, minus ₹650 CAC = −₹20 per order. Six weeks ago at ₹335 CAC you were making +₹295. The product and margin didn't change — only the ad's freshness did, and it's pushed you from healthy to barely underwater.

The lever: refresh the creative with genuinely new angles — new hook, new format, a different benefit — so the same audience gets something worth a second look. And set a cadence: rotate in new creative every couple of weeks so you never ride one winner until it dies. an0738.user: Panicking a bit — D2C jewellery and my ROAS is only 1.7, that feels terrible. Last 30 days: spend ₹8L, AOV ₹2,300, gross margin 68%, CAC ₹1,389, CTR 2.1%, and 90-day repeat is 41%. I feel like I should cut spend before I burn more cash. Tell me I'm not crazy.

The one caveat: watch CAC as you scale, because ₹1,389 will drift up when you expand past your best audiences, and your cushion is +₹175 on the first order.
